name: Parque México
blurb: An oval of jacarandas and palms wrapped around a duck pond, on the footprint of an old racetrack. The Art Deco Foro Lindbergh in the middle works as an informal scooter and skate plaza and spills into a play area.

name: Parque España
blurb: A block beyond Parque México and quieter, with a duck pond, a skate zone and swings. The Biblioteca Carlos Fuentes sits inside the park — a real children's library with air conditioning and a roof.

name: Jardín Ramón López Velarde
blurb: More an actual park than the Roma plazas — a basketball court, a skate area, fountains, a running circuit, playground equipment and an enclosed dog run strung along a long green spine.

name: Bosque de Chapultepec, Sección 1
blurb: The grand version of a city park: a real lake with rowboats for hire, a poet-lined promenade, and the Audiorama — a walled listening garden with curated music and free book loans, which is a very good place to park a sleeping stroller.

name: Parque Lincoln
blurb: Polanco's answer to Parque México, bigger and more manicured. A long reflecting pool where model boats are sailed at weekends, a 1937 clock tower, and the Abraham Lincoln aviary full of rescued and exotic birds.

name: Parque Hundido
blurb: A big unfussy park sunk into a former clay quarry, with replica pre-Hispanic sculpture scattered through the greenery. Roomier than the Condesa parks, with a small train, electric ride-ons and a bounce house on site.

name: Bosque de Tlalpan
blurb: A 253-hectare urban forest in the south of the city, with dedicated playgrounds, picnic areas and an outdoor theatre among the trees. Cooler and quieter than anything in the centre.

name: Parque Bicentenario
blurb: Fifty-five hectares built on a decommissioned refinery: a children's playground, three large greenhouses recreating Mexican ecosystems, an orchid garden, and boat rentals at weekends.

name: Alameda Central
blurb: The oldest public garden in the Americas, and still the place where city children strip down and run through the fountains on a hot day. Ten programmable fountains, century-old trees, wide flat promenades, and Bellas Artes at the far end.

name: Plaza Luis Cabrera
blurb: A Porfirian-era square built around a big central fountain and ringed by cafés with pavement tables. No play structure — the fountain is the attraction and running laps around it is the activity.

name: Plaza Villa de Madrid (Cibeles)
blurb: A replica of Madrid's Cibeles fountain marooned in a roundabout and surrounded by some of the better cafés in Roma. Handsome, shaded, photogenic.

name: Plaza Río de Janeiro
blurb: The postcard Roma square — a bronze David in the middle of a fountain, jacarandas, and grand crumbling mansions on every side.

name: Mercado Medellín
blurb: The Latin American market — five hundred vendors, heavy on Cuban, Colombian, Peruvian and Venezuelan sellers. Whole chickens and butchery on one side, pyramids of fruit and juice stands on the other, arepas and empanadas in between.

name: Mercado Michoacán
blurb: A 1946 Functionalist market building with street-art murals across its facades, and only twenty-seven stalls inside — a butcher, produce, a few prepared-food counters and a Café Toscano outpost.

name: Mercado Roma
blurb: A curated three-storey food hall rather than a produce market — Indian, Spanish-Mexican tapas, a juice bar, vegetarian tacos, and an ice cream counter, over cleaner floors than a working mercado.

name: Mercado de Coyoacán
blurb: A dense roofed warren where the smell of frying tostadas collides with fresh-cut mango and racks of embroidered blouses and piñatas. The tostada stalls at 181–182 are the reason people come.

name: Mercado de San Juan
blurb: The exotic-meats market chefs shop at — wild boar, venison, crocodile and ostrich in refrigerated cases, alongside imported cheese and charcuterie.

name: Maque
blurb: A neighbourhood panadería-cafetería that has been here since 1987 — pan dulce, pastries and coffee, with none of the queue that the famous bakeries attract.

name: Tout Chocolat
blurb: A chocolate-forward patisserie on the edge of Parque México — pastries, croissants and a house hot chocolate thick enough to stand a spoon in.

name: Cardinal Casa de Café
blurb: Specialty coffee with avocado toast and viennoiserie, indoors and on a terrace. The crowd skews calm and laptop-ish rather than rushed.

name: Chilpa
blurb: Creative chilaquiles and serious coffee, four minutes from the door. Someone who spent a week eating their way across the city called this their favourite breakfast of the trip.

name: Lázaro Focacceria
blurb: Specialty coffee and focaccia sandwiches, right next door to Chilpa — the option when pastries are not going to hold anybody until one o'clock.

name: Panadería Rosetta
blurb: The famous one — Elena Reygadas's bakery, and the guava-and-cardamom roll that launched a thousand imitations. Laminated croissants and seasonal fruit danishes alongside.

name: Forte
blurb: Specialty coffee with a cinnamon roll, a chocolate concha, breakfast tamales and a marinated-pork baguette. Dark, brick-lined, and easy to walk straight past — there is no sign.

name: Niddo
blurb: A full sit-down breakfast rather than a pastry counter — comfort food, an all-day breakfast menu, and baked goods alongside.

name: Churrería El Moro
blurb: Churros rolled in cinnamon sugar or filled with cajeta and chocolate, and the thick Mexican hot chocolate they are built to be dunked in.

name: Nevería Roxy
blurb: A 1946 soda fountain turned nevería, still scooping Mexican fruit ices — mamey, melon, guava, tamarind, zapote.

name: Merotoro
blurb: Baja Californian cooking — seafood and market produce — from Jair Téllez, two minutes from the front door.

name: Azul Condesa
blurb: Ricardo Muñoz Zurita's showcase of regional Mexican cooking — a flight of moles from seven regions, chiles en nogada in season, tamales and aguas frescas, à la carte rather than a tasting menu.

name: El Parnita
blurb: A gourmet taquería in a big plant-filled room under a greenhouse roof — arrachera and cochinita tacos, tuna tostadas, chicken cazuela, mezcal cocktails.

name: Fonda Fina
blurb: A modern take on the neighbourhood fonda — guacamole, pork-belly sopes, and a well-made mezcalrita, in a room everyone describes as warm rather than designed.

name: Lardo
blurb: Rosetta's Condesa sister — Mediterranean cooking with Mexican ingredients. Chilaquiles and pan dulce in the morning, courgette flowers and wood-fired pizza later.

name: Contramar
blurb: The city's defining seafood lunch: pescado a la talla — a butterflied snapper, half green parsley, half red adobo — and the tuna tostadas that every other restaurant in Mexico now serves a version of.

name: Meroma
blurb: A bright, high-ceilinged room doing precise seasonal cooking — described by someone who ate across the city as the best all-round restaurant there, elevated without being formal.

name: Rosetta
blurb: Elena Reygadas's restaurant in a restored Roma villa — Italian technique through Mexican ingredients, vegetable-forward, and the guava sourdough that people plan around.

name: Comedor Jacinta
blurb: Home-style Mexican cooking in a large open patio-like room — snail ceviche, an Oaxacan tlayuda with aged beef, mini gorditas with oxtail. The casual sister to a much more formal restaurant.

name: El Pescadito
blurb: Sonoran fried fish and shrimp tacos, with two absurd signatures: a cheese chile relleno stuffed with battered shrimp, and a marlin version of the same idea. Messy in the best way.

name: El Tizoncito
blurb: Widely credited as the birthplace of tacos al pastor — meat off the trompo with pineapple, onion and coriander, plus gringas and campechanos.

name: Tacos Hola El Güero
blurb: Open since 1968, twenty-two stewed fillings kept warm in ceramic pots — you order by pointing. The picadillo and the chorizo con papa are the ones to get, and the vegetable guisados are unusually good.

name: Taquería Orinoco
blurb: Monterrey-style trompo tacos, chicharrón, campechanos and queso fundido, in a proper sit-down room with a patio.

name: Lalo!
blurb: A bright, deliberately casual all-day room with long communal tables and a big open kitchen — the relaxed end of the Roma breakfast-and-lunch spectrum.

name: Baltra Bar
blurb: One of the most-loved cocktail bars in Condesa — small, dimly lit, Galápagos-themed, with a short and genuinely considered menu. Built for conversation rather than for being seen.

name: Diente de Oro
blurb: A whisky cantina with thirty-odd single malts, good music and a classic room that stops short of being stuffy. Sit-down, conversational, and pet-friendly.

name: El Ocho
blurb: A café-bar on the edge of Parque México with more than a hundred and twenty board games on the shelves, real cocktails, and food that runs to a hot dog buried under Doritos.

name: Lucky
blurb: A hotel rooftop with a genuine view over the Parque México canopy and a mezcal-forward cocktail list.

name: Licorería Limantour
blurb: Consistently ranked among the best cocktail bars in the world, and the reference point for the modern Mexico City drinks scene.

name: Papalote Museo del Niño
blurb: A cobalt-blue geometric cube visible across the park, holding five colour-coded halls built for climbing, pressing and splashing rather than reading. One of the best interactive children's museums in Latin America.

name: Zoológico de Chapultepec
blurb: Free, historic, and the first zoo outside China to breed giant pandas successfully. Xin Xin, the last giant panda in Latin America and the only one Mexico owns outright, turned thirty-six this month and is now in geriatric care.

name: Museo de Historia Natural
blurb: A cluster of white geodesic domes holding a full Diplodocus skeleton and a dinosaur puppet programme. Calmer and less overwhelming than the big Chapultepec draws.

name: Castillo de Chapultepec
blurb: The only castle in the Americas to have actually housed a sovereign. Period rooms, murals, and a terrace with the best single view over the Valley of Mexico.

name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
blurb: Twenty-three halls around a courtyard dominated by El Paraguas — a single vast concrete umbrella-column pouring water into the plaza, which tends to stop children in their tracks before they reach any exhibit.

name: Acuario Inbursa
blurb: Latin America's only underground aquarium — three subterranean levels, sharks passing overhead through a glass tunnel, jellyfish lit like lamps, and a touch pool that is reliably the highlight.

name: Aztlán Parque Urbano
blurb: The amusement park that replaced La Feria on the same ground, opened in 2024 — an eighty-five-metre Ferris wheel, a carousel, bumper cars, a butterfly garden and a planetarium.

name: Museo Frida Kahlo (Casa Azul)
blurb: Frida Kahlo's cobalt-blue childhood home, kept as she left it — her furniture, her wheelchair, her corsets, and paintings she never finished.

name: Jardín Centenario, Coyoacán
blurb: The shaded, tree-canopied heart of old Coyoacán, built around the Fuente de los Coyotes — the town's name means place of the coyotes. Clowns, bubble-blowers and balloon sellers work the square, heaviest at weekends.

name: Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares
blurb: A small, low-key museum of Mexican folk culture, and an artisan embroidery fair running 30 July to 2 August that adds a hands-on element to an otherwise text-heavy place.

name: Lucha Libre, Arena México
blurb: Masked luchadores, high-flying theatre and a crowd that treats the whole thing as pantomime, in the sport's home arena since 1956.

name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
blurb: A marble-and-glass opera house with an Art Deco interior, and Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros murals climbing the stairwells.

name: Torre Latinoamericana
blurb: A 1950s tower that survived every earthquake since, with an open-air observation deck forty-four floors up over the whole valley.

name: Zócalo
blurb: One of the largest city squares in the world, flanked by the cathedral and the National Palace, with an enormous flag raised at six in the morning and lowered at six in the evening.

name: Trajineras at Xochimilco
blurb: The canals are the last working remnant of the Aztec chinampa system — flat-bottomed painted boats poled past floating flower farms. On a weekday morning at Cuemanco it is genuinely quiet and beautiful.

name: Teotihuacán
blurb: The Avenue of the Dead running two kilometres between the Pyramids of the Sun and the Moon, built by a civilisation whose name for itself is lost.

name: Cuicuilco
blurb: A circular stepped pyramid two thousand years older than Teotihuacán, half-buried by a lava flow, sitting incongruously beside a ring road with a small site museum.

name: KidZania Cuicuilco
blurb: A miniature working city where children take jobs, earn currency and spend it — ninety-odd role-play establishments across fourteen thousand square metres, plus an outdoor track with kid-sized vehicles.

name: Tepoztlán
blurb: A mountain town under a wall of cliffs, with a sprawling craft and food market, a sixteenth-century monastery, and a pyramid on the ridge above.

name: Muévete en Bici
blurb: Every Sunday morning the city closes Paseo de la Reforma and a web of connecting avenues to cars, and tens of thousands of people ride, skate, walk and push prams down the middle of roads that are otherwise six lanes of traffic.

name: Bike Rentals Polanco
blurb: The only rental found in the city with verified child equipment actually on site — bikes with child seats, children's bikes, and cargo bikes with baskets.

name: Ecobici
blurb: The city bike share, with three stations within two minutes' walk. Sign up in the app; the nearest dock is on Aguascalientes at Insurgentes.

name: Juegos Infantiles, Parque Lincoln
blurb: The playground inside Parque Lincoln, under the trees at the eastern end, a couple of minutes from the aviary and the model-boat pond.

name: Aviario, Parque Lincoln
blurb: A walk-through aviary of rescued and exotic birds in the middle of Parque Lincoln, costing about eight pesos to enter.

name: La Bonvi
blurb: A contemporary taquería doing picaña, arrachera and New York strip on handmade tortillas, plus a spicy tuna tostada. The cachetada de picaña — thin beef under melted cheese with crisp edges — is the thing it is known for.

name: Quiasmo Coffee Bar
blurb: Specialty coffee two minutes from the door, open from six in the morning — espresso, pour-overs, and a cocoa with cardamom. Plenty of seating inside and a walk-up window if nobody wants to get out of the pushchair.

name: Emmer Panadería
blurb: French technique applied to Mexican classics — properly laminated croissants alongside conchas and flan, with a pour-over programme to match. A neighbourhood favourite rather than a queue-round-the-block destination.

name: Alfil
blurb: On the Roma Norte edge of Av. Sonora, a short walk up from the park.

name: Esquina Común
blurb: A corner restaurant in Condesa, a quarter of an hour on foot.

name: Castacán
blurb: Up in northern Roma. Castacán is the crisp pork belly cut, which suggests where the menu is pointed.

name: Kolobok Nápoles
blurb: A Russian restaurant in Nápoles — an entirely different proposition from everything else on this list, which is rather the point.

name: Skinday Facial Studio & Massage
blurb: Facials and massage in Roma Norte.

name: skin by Corrinne
blurb: A small studio in Juárez doing microchannelling, sugaring and tailored facials. Appointment only.

name: Skinbar by Gio
blurb: Facials with a Korean-skincare and face-yoga angle, somewhere in Roma Norte.
